title: Fossils: how rocks keep traces of dinosaurs and other old life

summary.text: A shell can lie inside a rock on a hill, far from any sea. It is a fossil: a trace of a being who lived long ago, kept in rock. Fossils show that dinosaurs lived on Earth for a very long time, and that the big ones died out about 66 million years ago. After them, mammals and birds spread into new kinds, and much later humans came. Your child presses hard and soft things into dough to see which leave a clear print, and digs down through a pile of old newspapers to see why deeper means older.
summary.art: A girl in a flat pressing a key and a steel spoon into a round of atta dough on a steel plate, with a banana slice and a coin beside it, and a poster of a dinosaur skeleton on the wall behind.

intro.hook: Nobody has ever seen a living dinosaur with a big tail and teeth. So how do we know they were real?
intro.text: We know from fossils. A fossil is a bone, a tooth, a shell, a footprint or a leaf print from long ago, kept in rock. Fossils are found in India too: dinosaur eggs in Gujarat, sea shells around Ariyalur in Tamil Nadu, and a stone tree trunk at Sattanur. In this unit you find out which things leave a fossil, and how we tell which fossils are older.
intro.art: A child holding up a small stone with the print of a coiled shell in it, looking at it closely, with a question mark drawn faintly above her head.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a fossil is, and name four kinds: bones, teeth, shells and footprints.
By the end I can say why hard parts like bones and shells become fossils more often than soft bodies, using my Print Test.
By the end I can say that deeper layers of rock are usually older than the layers on top.
By the end I can say what extinct means, and that the big dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.
By the end I can name animals that came after the dinosaurs, like mammals and birds, and say that humans are mammals too.
By the end I can say one thing scientists still argue about: what made the dinosaurs die out.

terms.meaning: A fossil is a trace of a living being from long ago, kept in rock. It can be a bone, a tooth, a shell, a leaf print or a footprint.
terms.example: A shell turned to stone in a hill near Ariyalur is a fossil.
terms.art: Four small pictures in a row: a bone in rock, a tooth, a coiled shell in stone, and a three-toed footprint in rock.

terms.meaning: A kind of animal or plant is extinct when every last one of that kind has died. They never come back.
terms.example: Mammoths are extinct. The last ones died about 4,000 years ago.
terms.art: A drawing of a woolly mammoth, faded grey, next to a living Indian elephant in full colour.

terms.meaning: Dinosaurs were a big family of reptiles who lived on land for about 165 million years. Some were huge, and some were as small as a hen.
terms.example: Rajasaurus was a meat-eating dinosaur whose bones were found in Gujarat.
terms.art: A big long-necked dinosaur and a small two-legged dinosaur the size of a hen, side by side.

terms.meaning: A palaeontologist is a scientist who studies fossils to find out about life long ago. Say it as pay-lee-on-tol-o-jist.
terms.example: A palaeontologist brushes dust off a dinosaur bone with a small paintbrush.
terms.art: A woman scientist kneeling by a rock, brushing a bone gently with a paintbrush, with a hat and a notebook beside her.

terms.meaning: A layer is one flat sheet lying on top of another. Rock often forms in layers, one on top of the next, over a very long time.
terms.example: The side of a hill can show stripes. Each stripe is a layer of rock.
terms.art: The side of a hill cut away, showing brown, cream and grey stripes of rock, one above the other.

terms.meaning: A trace fossil is a mark a living being left behind, not their body. Footprints, nests, burrows and tooth marks are trace fossils.
terms.example: A line of dinosaur footprints in rock is a trace fossil.
terms.art: A long line of three-toed footprints across a flat grey rock.

terms.meaning: A mammal is an animal with hair or fur who feeds their babies on milk. Cows, cats, elephants, whales and humans are mammals.
terms.example: A mother goat feeding her kid on milk is a mammal.
terms.art: A mother goat feeding a kid, a cat, an elephant and a small girl drinking milk from a tumbler.

terms.meaning: An asteroid is a big rock that travels through space around the Sun. A very large one hit the Earth 66 million years ago.
terms.example: The asteroid that hit the Earth then was about 10 kilometres wide.
terms.art: A rocky lump flying through dark space, with the blue Earth far away.

explanations.definition: A fossil is a trace of a living being from long ago, kept in rock.
explanations.description: When a living being dies, the body usually rots away or is eaten. Sometimes mud or sand covers it quickly. Over a very long time, the mud presses down and turns into rock. Water carries tiny bits of minerals into the bones or shell and turns them to stone, keeping their shape. Other fossils are only marks, like a footprint in mud that dried hard and was covered over. You made marks like these in your Print Test.
examples: A dinosaur bone that has turned to stone.
The print of a fern leaf in a dark rock.
A shell turned to stone in the limestone around Ariyalur, Tamil Nadu.
An insect caught in amber, which is tree resin that went hard. Amber about 50 million years old has been found in Gujarat.
explanations.context: This card is about what a fossil is and how a body or a mark can turn into one.
explanations.art: Three small scenes in order: a fish lying on the sea floor, mud covering the fish, and the fish's bones turned to stone inside a layer of rock.

explanations.concept: Why hard parts make most fossils
explanations.definition: Hard parts of a body, like bones, teeth, shells and wood, become fossils far more often than soft parts.
explanations.description: Soft parts rot away quickly or get eaten, by animals and by tiny living beings called bacteria. Hard parts last longer, so mud has time to cover them. In your Print Test, the key and the coin left sharp prints, and the banana and the tomato left blurry dents. So most fossils are bones, teeth and shells. Worms and jellyfish have lived in the sea for hundreds of millions of years, but we have found very few of their fossils.
examples: A shark's skeleton is made of soft cartilage, but its teeth are hard. Fossil shark teeth are common, and whole fossil sharks are rare.
An ammonite was a sea animal with a soft body and a coiled shell. We find the shells, and almost never the soft body.
Very rarely, soft bodies are kept too, when they are buried fast in very fine mud. Feathers and skin have been found this way.
explanations.context: This card explains your Print Test: why bones and shells become fossils, and soft bodies hardly ever do.
explanations.art: A round of dough with a sharp key print and a sharp spoon print beside a blurry, squashed banana mark.

explanations.definition: When layers pile up one on top of another, the layer at the bottom was laid down first, so it is the oldest.
explanations.description: Mud and sand settle at the bottom of rivers, lakes and seas. Each new layer lies on top of the last one. Over millions of years the layers turn into rock. So the deeper you dig, the further back in time you go, and a deep fossil is usually older than one above it. Your newspaper pile worked the same way: the oldest paper was at the bottom. Sometimes the Earth folds or tips the layers, and then scientists look for other clues.
examples: A pile of old newspapers waiting for the raddi collector has the oldest paper at the bottom.
The striped sides of a quarry show many layers, with the oldest at the bottom.
The Grand Canyon in the United States shows layers of rock almost two kilometres deep.
explanations.context: This card is about rock layers, and why the deeper fossils are usually older.
explanations.art: A cut-away hill with four stripes of rock. A shell fossil sits in the bottom stripe, a dinosaur bone in the middle, and a mammal's tooth near the top.

explanations.definition: Dinosaurs were a big family of reptiles who lived on land from about 230 million years ago.
explanations.description: There were many kinds of dinosaurs. Some ate plants, and some ate meat. Titanosaurs had very long necks and were among the biggest animals ever to walk on land. Some small dinosaurs had feathers, and all dinosaurs laid eggs. Their bones and eggs are found in Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu. The big dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. The first humans came only about 300,000 years ago, so people never met them.
examples: Rajasaurus, a meat-eater found in Gujarat. The name means king lizard.
Dinosaur eggs at Raiyoli, near Balasinor in Gujarat, found by scientists in 1981.
Sanajeh, a snake found coiled round a dinosaur egg in Gujarat. The fossil was found in 1984 and named in 2010.
explanations.context: This card is about the dinosaurs: who they were, and where in India their fossils are found.
explanations.art: A map of India with small drawings of a dinosaur egg in Gujarat, a bone in Madhya Pradesh and a coiled shell in Tamil Nadu.

explanations.concept: What made the big dinosaurs die out
explanations.description: About 66 million years ago, the big dinosaurs, the ammonites and many other kinds of life died out. Scientists agree on that. They still argue about why. A huge asteroid hit the Earth in what is now Mexico. At about the same time, giant volcanoes in western India poured out lava for thousands of years. Their rock still covers much of Maharashtra. Both could have filled the air with dust and gases, made the world dark and cold, and killed plants. Without plants, the plant-eaters starved, and then the meat-eaters.
examples: In 1980, Luis Alvarez, Walter Alvarez, Frank Asaro and the chemist Helen Michel found a thin layer of a rare metal called iridium in rocks of that age. Asteroids have much more iridium than the Earth's crust.
The Deccan Traps are the layers of old lava in western India. The Western Ghats near Mahabaleshwar are made of them.
The asteroid left a crater about 180 kilometres wide, called Chicxulub, now buried under the ground in Mexico.

perspectives.explanation: The asteroid was the main cause. The iridium layer and the giant crater both date to the very time the dinosaurs vanish.

perspectives.who: Gerta Keller, a scientist at Princeton University, and others
perspectives.explanation: The Deccan volcanoes in India were the main cause. They were already changing the air and the seas before the asteroid came.
Both mattered. The volcanoes made life harder, and the asteroid was the final blow.

explanations.context: This card is about a real argument: was it an asteroid, volcanoes in India, or both, that ended the big dinosaurs?
explanations.art: Two scenes side by side: a fiery rock falling from the sky into the sea, and red lava pouring out of the ground in hills.

explanations.definition: After the big dinosaurs died out, mammals and birds spread into many new kinds.
explanations.description: Mammals lived alongside the dinosaurs for millions of years. Most were small, about the size of a mouse or a rat. When the big dinosaurs were gone, there was room and food for others. Over millions of years, mammals became many new kinds: elephants, horses, bats, whales and, much later, humans. Some small dinosaurs lived on as birds, so the crow at your window is from the dinosaur family. Crocodiles, turtles, snakes, frogs and sharks also lived through the change.
examples: Indohyus was a small deer-like mammal whose fossils were found in Kashmir. Scientists think whales came from animals like them.
Mammoths were cousins of today's elephants. They lived until about 4,000 years ago, long after the dinosaurs.
Humans are mammals too. We feed babies on milk and have hair, like a cat or a cow.
explanations.context: This card is about the animals who came after the big dinosaurs, including us.
explanations.art: A short timeline from left to right: a big dinosaur, then a tiny furry mammal, then an elephant, a whale, a crow and a girl.

agreed.text: Fossils are the remains and traces of real beings who lived long ago.
agreed.evidence: Fossil bones have the same shapes as the bones of living animals, and fossil shells match living shells. We can see bone turning to stone, and footprints in rock are the same shape as footprints in mud.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: fossils are real traces of old life.

agreed.text: The big dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, and people came much later.
agreed.evidence: Dinosaur fossils are found only in rock layers older than 66 million years. Human fossils are found only in layers less than about 300,000 years old. No human fossil has ever been found with a big dinosaur.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: dinosaurs and people never met.

agreed.evidence: Fossils from China show small dinosaurs with feathers. Birds and these dinosaurs share many bones, like a wishbone and hollow bones.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: the crow at your window is a cousin of the dinosaurs.

challenging.claim: Dinosaurs were slow, cold, tail-dragging lizards.
challenging.for: Dinosaurs are reptiles, and most lizards today are slow when they are cold.
challenging.against: Most dinosaur trackways have no mark of a tail dragging behind. Many dinosaurs walked tall and fast, and some had feathers to keep warm.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of how dinosaurs moved.

challenging.claim: The dinosaurs were already dying out slowly before the asteroid hit.
challenging.for: In some places, fewer kinds of dinosaurs are found in the last few million years before the end.
challenging.against: Other scientists say we have found fewer fossils from those years, not fewer dinosaurs. In other places the dinosaurs look healthy right up to the end.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the dinosaurs were in trouble before the asteroid.

challenging.claim: A kind of animal can never die out completely.
challenging.who: Many thinkers in Europe before about 1800
challenging.for: They believed nature was complete and perfect, so no kind of being could be lost from it.
challenging.against: Georges Cuvier showed in 1796 that mammoths were a different kind from any living elephant. No one had ever seen one alive. Many kinds are gone, like the dodo of Mauritius.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that extinction cannot happen.

big_questions.q: Most animals who ever lived left no fossil at all. How can we find out about beings who left no trace?
big_questions.hint: Think about your Print Test. Which things left nothing? What other clues could there be?

big_questions.q: If the crow at the window comes from the dinosaurs, are the dinosaurs really all gone?
big_questions.hint: Think about what we mean by gone. Is a family gone if their great-great-grandchildren are still here?

big_questions.q: One day, far in the future, someone may dig up traces of us. What will they find, and what will they get wrong?
big_questions.hint: Think about which of our things are hard and last, like bones, coins and plastic, and which rot away.

big_questions.q: When a kind of animal dies out for ever, does the world lose something it cannot get back?
big_questions.hint: Think about the mammoth and the dodo, and the new kinds that came after the dinosaurs.

story.title: The Shell on the Hill
story.note: Kavya, Arjun, Meenakshi Athai and Selvi are made up. It is true that the limestone around Ariyalur in Tamil Nadu is full of fossil sea shells, including ammonites, and that the sea once covered that land. Ammonites died out at about the same time as the big dinosaurs.
text: Kavya was seven. Every summer she and her little brother Arjun went to stay with their aunt in Ariyalur, a small town in Tamil Nadu. Their aunt was called Meenakshi, and they called her Athai. Athai was a geologist. A geologist is a scientist who studies rocks.

Around Ariyalur the ground is full of limestone, a pale rock. Big machines dig it out to make cement. One morning Athai took them to the edge of an old quarry, where the digging had stopped long ago. The sides of the quarry had stripes. There was a cream stripe, a grey stripe, and a yellow stripe on top.
"Stay with me, and stay away from the edge," said Athai. "Now look at the ground by your feet."
Kavya crouched down. Among the pebbles was a round stone, as big as her palm. On it was a curl, going round and round like a coil of rope.
"A snail!" said Arjun. "A stone snail!"

"It looks like a snail," said Athai. "But this is the shell of an ammonite. Ammonites were sea animals. They had a soft body inside a coiled shell. Scientists think they had arms, a little like an octopus. This shell turned to stone a very long time ago."
Kavya frowned. "A sea animal? But the sea is far away from here. We came in a bus for hours."

"The sea is far away now," said Athai. "Long, long ago, the sea came right up to here. Ammonites swam in it. When they died, their shells sank to the sea floor. Mud and tiny shells piled on top of them, layer after layer. Over millions of years, the mud pressed down and turned into this limestone."
Kavya turned the stone over in her hands. She could see every ridge of the shell. "Where is the soft body, Athai? Where are the arms?"

"That is a good question," said Athai. "The soft body rotted away, or a fish ate the soft parts. Only the hard shell stayed long enough to be covered by mud. That is why we find so many shells in this rock, and almost no soft bodies."
Arjun picked up another stone. "Did a dinosaur eat the ammonite?"

"Ammonites lived at the same time as the dinosaurs," said Athai. "Dinosaurs lived on the land near here, and some of their bones have been found in this part of Tamil Nadu. But they did not swim in the sea. Big sea reptiles and fish hunted the ammonites."
"Can we see a living ammonite?" asked Arjun.

Athai shook her head. "No one can. Ammonites are extinct. That means every last one has died. They died out at about the same time as the big dinosaurs, about 66 million years ago. We know them only from their shells."

On the way back, they stopped at a tea shop. The woman who ran it, Selvi Akka, had a row of stones on her shelf. One had a coiled shell. One had a flat shell like a fan. "My father found these when he dug the well," she said. "Everyone round here finds them."
That night, Kavya could not sleep. She thought about the sea that was gone, and the ammonites that were gone. She thought about the soft arms that had rotted away.

In the morning, she found Athai making chapati dough in the kitchen. "Athai, can I have a bit?" Kavya pressed the dough flat on a steel plate. She pressed a spoon into it, then a curry leaf from the pot on the window, then a piece of banana from her breakfast.
She lifted them off one by one. The spoon left a smooth, sharp hollow. The curry leaf left a print with tiny lines, like the veins. The banana left only a squashed blob.
"Arjun, look!" Kavya called. "The hard things leave a good print. The soft banana just squashes. That is why we find the shells and not the arms!"
Arjun looked at the dough. Then he looked at his own hand. "Will my bones be a fossil one day?"
Kavya thought about it. "Maybe," she said, "if you lie down in some mud and wait a million years."
Arjun said he would rather have breakfast. Athai laughed, and gave them each a dosa. Then she wrapped the ammonite in a cloth, so Kavya could take it home to Chennai.
Outside the window, a crow landed on the ledge and looked at them. "Athai," said Kavya, "are all the dinosaurs gone, like the ammonites?"

Athai smiled and pointed at the crow. "Not all of them," she said. "Some small dinosaurs had feathers. Over millions of years, their grandchildren's grandchildren became the birds. So the crow is a cousin of the dinosaurs."
story.epiphany: Kavya sees that the shell stayed and the soft body did not, because hard parts last long enough to be covered by mud. Her dough shows the same thing: hard things leave a clear print, and soft things squash. So the rocks keep mostly shells and bones.
ask: Why was there a sea shell in a rock so far from the sea?
What happened to the ammonite's soft body?
What did Kavya's spoon, curry leaf and banana show her?
Athai said ammonites are extinct. What does extinct mean?
art: A woman geologist in a cotton sari and a wide hat standing with a girl and a small boy at the edge of a striped limestone quarry, keeping them back from the edge.
A girl crouching, holding a round stone with a coiled ammonite shell on it, while her little brother points at it.
A small tea shop with a row of fossil stones on a shelf, and a smiling woman behind the counter.
A girl in a kitchen lifting a curry leaf off a flat round of dough on a steel plate, with a spoon print and a squashed banana mark beside it, and a crow on the window ledge.

games.title: Fossil Clues: what does this fossil tell us?
games.players: 2 to 4 players. A grown-up can be one of them.
games.context: In this game each card shows a fossil that a scientist found. You say what you think the fossil tells us about life long ago. The answer is on the back.

items.f: A line of footprints in rock, each with three long toes.
items.b: A dinosaur walked here, over soft mud that later turned to rock.

img.credit: Anne S. Schulp, Mohammed Al-Wosabi and Nancy J. Stevens, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

items.f: A sea shell inside a rock on a hill, far from the sea.
items.b: The sea once covered this land.

items.f: Big, sharp, curved teeth, with tiny ridges like a saw.
items.b: The animal ate meat. Sharp teeth cut through flesh.

items.f: Flat, wide teeth with rough tops.
items.b: The animal ate plants. Flat teeth grind up leaves.

items.f: Many dinosaur eggs in nests close together, in Gujarat.
items.b: Many dinosaur mothers laid their eggs in the same place.

items.f: A snake curled round a dinosaur egg, found in Gujarat.
items.b: A snake like this one may have hunted baby dinosaurs. This snake is called Sanajeh.

items.f: The print of a leaf, with all its veins, in a dark rock.
items.b: Plants grew here. The leaf fell into mud before it rotted.

items.f: Footprints of the same dinosaur, very far apart.
items.b: The dinosaur was moving fast. Longer steps mean faster.

items.f: A whole tree trunk made of stone, at Sattanur in Tamil Nadu.
items.b: A forest grew here long ago. Minerals in water slowly turned the wood to stone.

items.f: An insect trapped inside a clear yellow lump.
items.b: Sticky tree resin trapped the insect, then went hard. This is called amber.

items.f: Feathers pressed into a rock, next to small dinosaur bones.
items.b: Some dinosaurs had feathers. Birds come from dinosaurs like these.

items.f: A rock with no fossils in it at all.
items.b: That does not mean nothing lived there. Soft bodies rot away and leave no trace.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, words up.
On your turn, take the top card and read it aloud. A grown-up reads it if you cannot.
Say what the fossil tells us about life long ago, and why.
The player next to you turns the card over and reads the back. If your idea matches, you keep the card.
If it does not match, put the card in a middle pile. Read the back aloud so everyone learns it.
The game ends when the pile is gone. The player with the most cards wins. If two players have the same number, they both win.

setup.art: A pile of small clue cards on a floor mat, with three children and a grown-up sitting round it.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cards in a pile, words up.

setup.art: A girl holding a card that says a sea shell inside a rock on a hill, with a thinking face, and the answer side turned towards the grown-up.
setup.caption: 2. Say what the fossil tells us. Then turn the card over to check.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. Read the rules aloud. 3. Decide who goes first.
flow.say: Scientists who study fossils are like detectives. A fossil is a clue. Let us see what each clue tells us.
flow.kid: Each card is a fossil clue. Say what it tells us. Then check the back.

flow.do: 1. Take turns with the cards. 2. Ask for a reason each time. 3. The next player turns the card over to check.
flow.say: A sea shell in a rock on a hill. What does that tell us? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Read the card. Say what it tells us. Say why. Turn it over.

ask.q: Why can't we say nothing lived where a rock has no fossils?
good: Maybe they were soft, like worms.

flow.parent: Accept any answer that fits the clue, even if the words differ from the back. The last card, the rock with no fossils, is the hardest. Link it to the Print Test if your child has done it. If you play with one child, you take turns too, and your child reads your backs.

flow.do: Count the cards each player kept, then ask the last question.
flow.say: Count your cards. Which clue was the biggest surprise? Why?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Which clue surprised you most?

check.q: A fossil shows big, sharp, curved teeth with ridges like a saw. What does it tell us about the animal?
options: The animal lived in a nest
check.why: Sharp teeth with ridges cut through flesh, so the animal ate meat. Flat teeth grind leaves.

games.title: Who Lived Through the Big Change?
games.players: 1 to 4 players. A grown-up can be one of them.
games.context: Sixty-six million years ago the world suddenly became dark and cold, and many plants died. In this game you look at animals who were alive then, and guess who lived through it. The answer is on the back.

items.f: Tyrannosaurus rex. Huge. Ate only meat, and needed a lot of it.
items.b: Died out. There was not enough food for such a big meat-eater.

img.credit: USDAgov, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

items.f: A tiny furry mammal, about the size of a mouse. Ate insects and seeds. Hid in burrows.
items.b: Lived through it. Small mammals could hide underground and eat many kinds of food.

items.f: A crocodile. Lived in rivers. Could go for months without eating.
items.b: Lived through it. Crocodiles are still here today.

img.credit: Mike Prince, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: A turtle. Lived in ponds and rivers, and could rest for a long time.
items.b: Lived through it. Turtles are still here today.

items.f: A small bird who lived on the ground and ate seeds.
items.b: Lived through it. Some birds survived, and scientists think they were small ground birds who could eat seeds.

items.f: An ammonite. A sea animal with a coiled shell.
items.b: Died out. Every kind of ammonite was gone.

img.credit: Becks, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.f: A titanosaur. A long-necked dinosaur, one of the biggest land animals ever. Ate huge amounts of plants.
items.b: Died out. When the plants died, there was not enough food.

items.f: A pterosaur. A flying reptile with skin wings, not a bird.
items.b: Died out. Every kind of pterosaur was gone.

items.f: A frog. Lived in ponds and could hide in the mud.
items.b: Lived through it. Frogs are still here today.

img.credit: Haneesh K M, CC0, via iNaturalist

items.f: A small snake. Could hide in holes and go a long time without food.
items.b: Lived through it. Snakes are still here today.

items.f: A shark. Lived in the sea and ate many kinds of food.
items.b: Lived through it. Many sharks died, but some kinds lived on.

items.f: A mosasaur. A huge sea reptile who hunted big fish and ammonites.
items.b: Died out. The sea animals they hunted were disappearing.

printables.title: 2 mat labels to put on the floor

rules: Put the two mat labels on the floor: Lived through it, and Died out.
Shuffle the animal cards and put them in a pile, words up.
On your turn, take the top card and read it aloud. A grown-up reads it if you cannot.
Say which mat it goes on, and why. Put the card on that mat.
The player next to you turns the card over and reads the back. If you were right, make a tally mark for yourself on the paper.
If you were wrong, move the card to the right mat. Nobody loses a point.
When the pile is gone, the player with the most tally marks wins. Then look at the Lived through it mat. What do those animals have in common?

setup.art: Two sheets of paper on a floor, labelled Lived through it and Died out, with a pile of animal cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the two mats and the pile of cards.

setup.art: A child putting a card about a tiny furry mammal on the Lived through it mat, while a grown-up holds the next card.
setup.caption: 2. Put each card on a mat, then turn it over to check.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards and the two mat labels. 2. Lay the mat labels on the floor. 3. Draw a tally box for each player on a sheet of paper. 4. Tell your child about the big change.
flow.say: Long ago, the sky went dark for a long time. It got cold, and many plants died. Which animals do you think lived through it?
flow.kid: The world went dark and cold. Many plants died. Who lived through it?

flow.do: 1. Take turns with the cards. 2. Ask for a reason each time. 3. The next player turns the card over to check.
flow.say: A tiny furry mammal who hid in burrows. Which mat? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Read the card. Pick a mat. Say why. Turn it over.

ask.q: Why did the huge plant-eaters die out?
good: The plants died, so they had no food.
They were too big to find enough food.

flow.parent: There is no shame in a wrong guess here. Scientists were surprised too. Help your child notice the pattern: small, able to hide, able to eat many foods, or able to go a long time without food.

flow.do: Look at the two mats together and ask the last question.
flow.say: Look at the animals who lived through it. What do many of them have in common?
flow.kid: Look at the Lived through it mat. How are those animals alike?

check.q: Which kind of animal had the best chance in the big change?
options: A small animal who could hide and eat many foods
A huge animal who ate only one kind of food
A flying reptile with skin wings
check.why: Small animals need less food, and can hide in burrows or water. Animals who can eat many foods can find something to eat when their usual food is gone.

experiments.title: The Print Test: which things leave a fossil print?
experiments.context: In this experiment you press eight things into flat rounds of dough, four hard and four soft. Then you look at the prints they leave. A print in mud is how many fossils begin.
experiments.question: When we press hard things and soft things into dough in the same way, which ones leave a clear print?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which of the eight things will leave the clearest print? Which will leave the worst? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every thing is pressed into the same dough, rolled to the same thickness. Each one is covered with the same steel plate and pressed for a count of 10. Each is lifted straight up. Only the thing we press changes.

materials.item: 2 cups of atta, a little water and a pinch of salt, kneaded into a stiff dough
4 hard things: a coin, a key, a steel spoon, and a sea shell or a tamarind seed
4 soft things: a slice of banana, a piece of ripe tomato, a piece of idli or soft bread, and a wet ball of cotton wool
a steel plate or a flat lid, to press with
a rolling pin, or a steel tumbler on its side
a sheet of paper and a pencil for the table

schedule.what: Guess. Make eight dough rounds. Sort the things into hard and soft. Press each one. Score each print. Talk about what you saw.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all eight things. Draw the clearest print and the blurriest print under it.

setup.art: Eight small rounds of atta dough on a steel plate, each about as thick as a finger, with a rolling pin beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Roll the dough and make eight flat rounds.

setup.art: A child's hands placing a key on one dough round and a banana slice on another, with a coin, a spoon, a tomato piece, idli and cotton waiting in a row.
setup.caption: 2. Put one thing on each round.

setup.art: A child pressing a steel plate down with both hands on top of a dough round, counting to ten.
setup.caption: 3. Cover with the plate and press for a count of 10.

setup.art: Eight dough rounds in two rows. The top row shows a sharp key, coin, spoon and seed print. The bottom row shows four blurry, squashed marks.
setup.caption: 4. Lift each thing off and look at the print.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the eight things. 2. Ask which will leave the clearest print, and why. 3. Write the guess at the top of the sheet.
flow.say: We are going to press each of these into dough. Which one will leave the clearest print? Which will leave the worst? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the eight things. Which will leave the best print? Why?

ask.q: Which do you think will leave the clearest print?
good: The key, because it is hard.
The banana, because it is big.
The coin, because it is heavy.

flow.parent: Write down any guess and say nothing yet. Many children pick the biggest or heaviest thing. The test will show them what matters.

flow.do: 1. Roll the dough out on the counter until it is about as thick as your child's finger. 2. Cut or pull it into eight rounds, each about the size of your palm. 3. Lay them on a plate or a clean counter.
flow.say: Let us roll the dough, all the same thickness. Then we make eight rounds, one for each thing.
flow.kid: Roll the dough flat. Make eight rounds, all the same size.
flow.parent: If the dough sticks to things, dust the top with a little dry atta. Stiff dough gives the clearest prints, so use only a little water.

flow.do: 1. Your child squeezes each thing gently between finger and thumb. 2. Put the four hard things in one row and the four soft things in another.
flow.say: Squeeze each one gently. Does it squash, or does it stay the same shape? Put the hard ones here and the soft ones there.
flow.kid: Squeeze each one gently. Hard ones in this row. Soft ones in that row.
flow.parent: Let your child decide which row each thing goes in, and talk about it. A steel spoon is hard. Cotton wool feels soft.

flow.do: 1. Put one thing on each round. 2. Cover it with the steel plate. 3. Your child presses down with both hands and counts to 10. 4. Lift the plate, then lift the thing straight up.
flow.say: Put the plate on top. Press with both hands while we count to ten. Now lift it straight up, slowly.
flow.kid: Put the plate on top. Press hard and count to ten. Lift it straight up.

ask.q: What happened to the banana when you pressed it?
good: It went mushy and stuck to the dough.

flow.parent: Press each thing the same way, so the test is fair. Pick soft things off with a spoon if they stick.

flow.do: 1. Look at each print together. 2. For each one, write clear, blurry or none in the table. 3. Look at the key print closely for its small lines.
flow.say: Look at each print. Can you see the shape clearly? Can you see any tiny lines? Is it clear, blurry, or nothing at all?
flow.kid: Look at each print. Is it clear, blurry or nothing? Fill in the table.

check.q: Which row of prints was clearer?
check.why: Hard things keep their shape when pressed, so they push a sharp print into the dough. Soft things squash and spread, so their prints are blurry.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why. 2. Then read the explanation card on why hard parts make most fossils.
flow.say: Was your guess right? What did you see? Why do you think the hard things left better prints?
flow.kid: Was your guess right? Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Why do we find so many fossil bones and shells, and so few fossil worms?
good: Bones and shells are hard, so they leave a good print and last.
Worms are soft, so they squash and rot away.

flow.parent: Listen to the reason before you explain. A strong answer says that hard things keep their shape, while soft things squash and rot. Throw away the dough that touched the fruit and the cotton.
flow.think: Your bones are hard. Your skin is soft. Which part of you would the rocks keep?

activities.title: The Newspaper Pile: dig down through time
activities.context: In this activity you dig down through a pile of old newspapers, the way a scientist digs down through rock layers. You read the date on each paper to find out which layer is oldest.

materials.item: a pile of old newspapers or magazines with dates on them, at least 7, like the pile kept for the raddi collector
3 small things to bury: a leaf, a bus ticket or a bill, and a sweet wrapper
a sheet of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Guess where the oldest paper is. Dig down and read each date. Find the buried things and say which is oldest.

activities.record: A list of the dates from top to bottom, with a star next to each place you found a buried thing.

setup.art: A neat pile of folded newspapers on a floor, with a leaf poking out near the bottom and a bus ticket near the middle.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up hides three things at different depths in the pile.

setup.art: A child lifting the top newspaper off the pile and pointing to the date printed at the top of the page.
setup.caption: 2. Lift off one paper at a time, and read its date.

setup.art: A child's sheet with a list of dates going down the page, and stars next to three of them.
setup.caption: 3. Write the dates in order, and star where each thing was.

flow.do: 1. Stack the newspapers with the oldest at the bottom. 2. Slip the leaf in near the bottom. 3. Put the ticket in the middle and the wrapper near the top, while your child is not looking. 4. Ask your child the question.
flow.say: This pile grew one paper a day. Which paper do you think is the oldest, the top one or the bottom one? Why?
flow.kid: This pile grew one paper each day. Is the oldest one at the top or the bottom? Why?
flow.parent: If your pile has been mixed up, sort the papers by date first, with the newest on top. The activity only works if the pile grew in order. Pretend that each paper came on a different day, and that the three small things fell into the pile on the days they were put in.

flow.do: 1. Your child lifts off one paper at a time. 2. Read the date together, and your child writes it on the list. 3. When a buried thing turns up, your child draws a star next to the date of the paper just above it.
flow.say: Lift off the top paper. What date does it say? Write it down. Now the next one.
flow.kid: Lift off one paper. Read the date. Write it down. Do the next one.

ask.q: Are the dates getting older or newer as you dig down?
good: Older. Each paper down is from an earlier day.

flow.do: 1. Look at the list and the stars together. 2. Ask which buried thing is the oldest.
flow.say: Look at the dates next to the stars. Which thing is under the oldest papers? That one fell into the pile first. How do you know?
flow.kid: Which thing was buried first? How do you know?

check.q: A scientist finds one fossil deep down and another near the top. Which is usually older?
check.why: Layers pile up one on top of another, so the deeper layers were laid down first. A fossil deep down is usually older.

flow.parent: This is how scientists tell which fossils are older. Rock layers pile up like newspapers, with the oldest at the bottom.
flow.think: Rock layers take thousands of years to pile up. Newspapers take one day each. What else in our home piles up in layers?

activities.title: Footprint Detective: what can footprints tell us?
activities.context: In this activity you make wet footprints on newspaper, once walking slowly and once taking big quick steps. Then you see how far apart the prints are. Scientists read dinosaur footprints in rock the same way.
activities.safety: Walk, do not run. Tape the ends of the newspaper so it does not slide on a smooth floor. Dry your feet before stepping off the paper.

materials.item: 8 sheets of newspaper, opened out and laid end to end in two lines of 4 sheets, with the ends taped to the floor
a flat steel plate or tray with a little water in it, and a towel
a ruler, or your hand span to measure with

schedule.what: Make wet footprints walking slowly on the first line, then with big quick steps on the second line. Measure the gaps and compare.

activities.record: Write how many hand spans apart the slow prints were, and how many the quick prints were.

setup.art: Two long lines of newspaper sheets taped to the floor of a flat's corridor, with a steel plate of water at one end and a towel at the other.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the newspaper in two lines, with water at one end.

setup.art: A child stepping slowly along the newspaper with wet feet, leaving dark footprints close together.
setup.caption: 2. Walk slowly along the paper.

setup.art: Two lines of wet footprints on newspaper, one with prints close together and one with prints far apart, and a hand span measuring a gap.
setup.caption: 3. Take big quick steps on the second line. Measure the gaps.

flow.do: 1. Lay the newspaper in two lines and tape the ends. 2. Put the plate of water and the towel at the start of the first line. 3. Ask the question.
flow.say: When you walk fast, will your footprints be closer together or farther apart than when you walk slowly? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Walk slow, then walk fast. Will the prints be closer or farther apart? Why?

flow.do: 1. Your child dips both feet in the water and walks slowly along the first line. 2. Then they dry their feet and stand at the start of the second line. 3. They dip again and walk with big quick steps, without running.
flow.say: Dip your feet and walk slowly along the paper. Now dry your feet. This time take big, quick steps, but do not run.
flow.kid: Dip your feet. Walk slowly. Dry your feet. Now take big quick steps.
flow.parent: The wet prints fade in a minute or two, so measure them straight away. Hold your child's hand if the paper feels slippery.

flow.do: 1. In each line, measure from the heel of one print to the heel of the next. 2. Use hand spans or a ruler. 3. Write both numbers down.
flow.say: How many hand spans between your slow steps? How many between your quick steps?
flow.kid: Measure the gaps with your hand. Which gaps are bigger?

check.q: Your quick steps were farther apart. A dinosaur's footprints in rock are very far apart. What does that tell us?
check.why: Faster walking or running makes longer steps. Scientists use the gaps between fossil footprints to work out how fast a dinosaur was moving. A bigger dinosaur also takes longer steps, so scientists look at the size of the foot too.

flow.do: Ask what else the footprints show.
flow.say: Look at the prints again. What else could a detective tell about you from them?
flow.kid: What else do your footprints tell about you?

ask.q: What else do your prints show?
good: That I walk on two legs.

flow.parent: Footprints are trace fossils. A trace fossil is a mark an animal left, not their body. Dinosaur trackways have been found in many places around the world.

projects.title: My Fossil Museum: salt dough prints that last
projects.context: In this project you make fossil prints in salt dough, dry them for two days until they are hard, and set up a small fossil museum at home with a label for each one.

materials.item: 1 cup of atta or maida, half a cup of salt and about half a cup of water, mixed into a stiff dough
4 hard things to press: a shell, a coin, a key, and a toy animal's foot
a sunny windowsill or a warm shelf for drying
small pieces of card and a pencil for labels

schedule.what: Make the salt dough. Press four things into four rounds. Lift them out and put the rounds to dry.
Turn the rounds over so the bottoms dry too. Press gently with a finger. Are they getting hard?
Write a label for each fossil. Set up the museum on a shelf and show someone at home round it.

projects.record: Four hard prints, each with a label saying what made it and what it tells a visitor.

setup.art: A child pressing a shell into a round of pale salt dough on a plate, with three more rounds waiting.
setup.caption: 1. Press a hard thing into each round of salt dough.

setup.art: Four salt dough prints drying on a sunny windowsill.
setup.caption: 2. Dry the prints in a warm place for two days.

setup.art: A small shelf museum with four hard dough fossils, each with a handwritten card label, and a relative looking at them.
setup.caption: 3. Label each fossil and show someone at home round.

flow.do: 1. Mix the flour and salt, then add water a little at a time until the dough is stiff. 2. Make four rounds about half a finger thick, so they dry faster. 3. Press one hard thing into each round and lift it out.
flow.say: Salt dough goes hard when it dries, a bit like mud turning to rock. Press each thing in firmly, then lift it straight out.
flow.kid: Make four rounds. Press one hard thing into each. Lift it out.

flow.wait: Leave the prints to dry for a day
flow.do: 1. Gently turn each round over. 2. Press gently on the edge to feel if it is hard.
flow.say: Feel the edge. Is it harder than yesterday? Real mud takes a very long time to turn to rock.
flow.kid: Turn each one over. Is it getting hard?

flow.wait: Leave the prints to dry for one more day
flow.do: 1. Your child writes a label for each print: what made it, and one thing it tells. 2. Set them out on a shelf. 3. Your child shows someone at home round the museum.
flow.say: Write what made each print. Then add one thing a visitor can learn from it. Who will you show round your museum?
flow.kid: Write a label for each fossil. Show someone your museum.

ask.q: What does your museum visitor learn from one of your prints?
good: The print was made by a shell with ridges, so we can tell what made it.

flow.parent: A good label says what made the print and what it tells us, like a real museum. If the prints are still soft on day three, leave them one more day in the sun.

challenges.title: A Footprint That Lasts
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Real fossil footprints lasted millions of years. Your job is to make a print that is still clear two days later, even after a few drops of water fall on it.
challenges.problem: Make a print of your thumb or a toy animal's foot that still looks clear two days later, after you sprinkle five drops of water on it.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
It must be a print, pressed in, not a drawing.
Two days later you sprinkle five drops of water on it, and it must still be clear.
materials: a little school glue, if you have it
a little soil from a plant pot, mixed with water into mud
a toy animal, or your thumb
general: Let the print dry hard on a sunny windowsill for two days before the water test.
Use salt dough, which goes harder than plain atta dough. Make it about half a finger thick so it dries faster.
Make the print deep, so a little water cannot smooth it out.
creative: Let a salt dough print dry hard, then brush a thin coat of school glue over it. Glue dries hard and keeps water out.
Sprinkle a thin layer of dry atta over the dried print to cover it, the way new mud covers a real footprint. Brush it off gently before the water test.
Press the print into thick mud from a plant pot. Dry the mud in the sun. Mud dries hard, like the mud of a real footprint.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way to make a print last. Test it against one of the ideas above. Which one stayed clearer?

setup.art: A child pressing a toy dinosaur's foot into a round of dough, a patch of mud and a small patch of mud on a plate.
setup.caption: 1. Make the same print in two or three materials.

setup.art: A child sprinkling drops of water from her fingers onto three dried prints two days later.
setup.caption: 2. Two days later, sprinkle five drops on each and look.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem aloud. 2. Your child picks two or three materials to try.
flow.say: Real footprints in mud lasted millions of years. Can you make a print that is still clear tomorrow, even after some water?
flow.kid: Make a print that lasts until tomorrow. Even after drops of water.

flow.do: 1. Your child makes the same print in each material. 2. Put them all on a sunny windowsill to dry.
flow.say: Make the same print in each one, pressed in the same way. Then let them dry.
flow.kid: Make the same print in each one. Let them dry.

flow.wait: Leave the prints for two days
flow.do: 1. Sprinkle five drops of water on each print. 2. Wait one minute and look. 3. Talk about which lasted best, and why.
flow.say: Five drops on each. Now look. Which print is still clear? Why do you think that one lasted?
flow.kid: Put five drops on each. Which print is still clear? Why?

check.q: Five drops of water fall on a print that dried hard and on a print left soft and wet. Which is more likely to stay clear?
options: The print left soft and wet
check.why: A print that has dried hard keeps its shape. Real footprints that lasted millions of years dried hard in the sun, and then were covered by new mud.

items.p: Which one of these is a fossil?
opts: The print of a shell in a rock
A new shell picked up on the beach today
items.why: A fossil is a trace of a being from long ago, kept in rock. A toy was never alive, and a new shell is not old or in rock.

items.p: Draw the clearest print and the blurriest print from your Print Test. Write under each one what made it.
items.a: Two drawings, a sharp print of a hard thing and a blurry print of a soft thing, each labelled.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the sharp edges and lines of the hard thing's print, and the smudged shape of the soft thing's print.

items.p: Sort these into two groups: Often becomes a fossil, and Hardly ever becomes a fossil.
items.why: Teeth, shells and bones are hard, so they last long enough to be buried. Jellyfish, earthworms and slugs are soft, so they rot away first.

items.p: People and the big dinosaurs lived on Earth at the same time.
items.why: False. The big dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. The first humans came about 300,000 years ago.

items.p: Draw a line from each fossil to what it tells us.
pairs: A sea shell in a hill
The sea once covered this land
items.why: Each fossil is a clue. Footprints show how an animal moved, teeth show what they ate, eggs show how babies began, and sea shells show where the sea was.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down. In your Print Test, why did the banana slice not leave a sharp print?
items.a: The banana is soft. It squashed and spread out when I pressed it, so its edges were not sharp.
items.why: A strong answer says the banana is soft, so it changed shape when pressed instead of pushing its shape into the dough.

items.p: Nila, a girl in Class 2, and her brother Ravi are talking about dinosaurs.

views.says: All the dinosaurs are gone. They died out 66 million years ago.
Not all of them. Birds come from dinosaurs, so the crow on our window is a kind of dinosaur.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Say why. Then say one thing the other child is right about.
items.a: Both are partly right. The big dinosaurs, like Rajasaurus and the titanosaurs, all died out. But some small feathered dinosaurs lived on, and birds come from them.
items.why: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and sees that it depends on what we mean by dinosaurs: the big ones are gone, and the birds are their family.

items.p: Here is the side of a hill with three layers of rock. Write 1 on the oldest layer and 3 on the newest layer.
items.a: 1 on the bottom layer, 2 on the middle layer and 3 on the top layer.
items.why: Layers pile up one on top of another, so the bottom one was laid down first and is the oldest. Your newspaper pile showed the same thing.
items.art: The side of a hill with three stripes of rock: a grey bottom stripe with a shell fossil, a brown middle stripe with a bone, and a cream top stripe with a small tooth.

items.p: Soft bodies, like a jellyfish, hardly ever become fossils, because they ________ away before mud can cover them.
items.why: Soft bodies rot away or are eaten quickly. Hard parts last long enough to be buried.

items.p: Asha, a girl in Class 2, makes a pile of 7 newspapers, one for each day of a week, with the oldest at the bottom. She hides a leaf under the 3rd paper from the top. How many papers are under the leaf?
items.why: 7 papers in all, and 3 are above the leaf. 7 take away 3 is 4. So 4 papers are under the leaf, and they are older than the leaf's day.

items.p: Scientists still argue about what made the big dinosaurs die out 66 million years ago.

views.says: A huge asteroid hit the Earth, in what is now Mexico. That was the main cause.

views.who: Gerta Keller, a scientist, and others
views.says: Giant volcanoes in western India poured out lava for thousands of years. They were the main cause.
Both. The volcanoes made life hard, and the asteroid finished it.

items.ask: Which do you think is right? Give one reason. Then say what someone on another side might answer.
items.a: Any side, with a reason. For the asteroid: a giant crater and a layer of iridium date to that very time. For the volcanoes: the Deccan lava poured out around the same time and changed the air. For both: they happened close together.
items.why: A strong answer picks a side, gives a piece of evidence, and fairly says one point from another side. Nobody knows for sure yet.

items.p: Put these in order, from longest ago to most recent.
items.why: The first dinosaurs lived about 230 million years ago. The big ones died out about 66 million years ago. The last mammoths lived about 4,000 years ago. You were born only a few years ago.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 2, finds a fossil sea shell in a rock on a hill in Ariyalur, far from the sea. What does this tell her about that place? Say it, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: The sea once covered that land, long ago. The shell sank into the mud on the sea floor, and the mud turned to rock.
items.why: A strong answer says the sea used to be there, and explains how a sea shell came to be inside rock.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? Elephant, whale, Tyrannosaurus rex, human.
items.why: Elephants, whales and humans are mammals, who came after the big dinosaurs. Tyrannosaurus rex was a dinosaur.

items.p: Draw an animal who is alive today. Draw a ring round the parts that would most likely become a fossil.
items.a: A drawing of an animal with rings round the bones, teeth, shell, horns or claws.
items.why: A strong answer rings the hard parts, like teeth, bones, horns, claws or a shell, because hard parts last long enough to become fossils.

items.p: A scientist finds the print of a leaf in a rock in a very dry place. What does it tell us?
opts: The leaf fell from a tree today
items.why: A leaf print is a trace of a plant. The plant lived there long ago, even if the place is dry now.

items.p: Every animal who dies becomes a fossil.
items.why: False. Most bodies rot or are eaten before mud can cover them. Only a tiny few become fossils, and those are mostly the hard parts.

items.p: Anjali, a girl in Class 2, says: 'The dinosaurs died out because they were stupid and slow.' What would you tell her? Say it, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: The dinosaurs lived on Earth for about 165 million years, so they were very good at living. They died out because the world changed suddenly, and many could not find enough food.
items.why: A strong answer says the dinosaurs did well for a very long time, and that a sudden change, not being slow or stupid, ended the big ones. Many fast and clever animals died too.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to what is true about them.
pairs: A bird, from the dinosaur family
A mammal, who came after the dinosaurs
A reptile who lived with the dinosaurs and is still here
A sea animal with a shell, now extinct
items.why: Birds come from dinosaurs. Elephants are mammals who spread after the dinosaurs. Crocodiles lived through the big change. Ammonites died out.

items.p: Sort these into two groups: Still alive today, and Extinct.
items.why: Crocodiles, turtles and crows are alive today. Ammonites, Tyrannosaurus rex and mammoths are extinct.

videos.title: How a fossil forms
videos.why: Shows a body being covered by mud and slowly turning to stone, which a child cannot see happen at home.
videos.check: Found by search: "How do dinosaur fossils form?" by Natural History Museum, 3 min 49 s. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Balasinor Dinosaur Museum, Gujarat
videos.why: Shows the dinosaur fossil park and museum at Balasinor in Gujarat, where real dinosaur eggs and bones were found in India.
videos.check: Found by search: "Balasinor Dinosaur Museum - Enter into the World of Dinosaurs" by Gujarat Tourism, 4 min 10 s. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: What happened when the asteroid hit
videos.why: Looks at the asteroid and the Deccan volcanoes as causes of the dinosaurs dying out, and shows that scientists still study the cause.
videos.check: Found by search: "What Exactly Killed The Dinosaurs? | Earth | BBC Earth Science" by BBC Earth Science, 3 min 55 s. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 2, finds the shape of a leaf in a dark rock. What is it?
quiz.why: A leaf print kept in rock is a fossil, a trace of a plant from long ago.

quiz.p: Which of these is a trace fossil?
quiz.why: A trace fossil is a mark an animal left behind, not their body. A footprint is a mark.

quiz.p: Why do we find many fossil bones but very few fossil worms?
opts: Worms are soft and rot away
Worms did not live long ago
quiz.why: Worms have lived for hundreds of millions of years. Their soft bodies rot away before mud can turn to rock round them.

quiz.p: In the Print Test, Meena, a girl in Class 2, pressed a key and a tomato into dough. What did she see?
opts: The key left a sharp print, and the tomato left a blurry one
The tomato left the sharpest print
quiz.why: The key is hard and keeps its shape. The tomato is soft, so it squashes and spreads.

quiz.p: In a cliff, a fossil is found in the bottom layer and another in the top layer. Which is older?
opts: The one in the bottom layer
The one in the top layer
quiz.why: Layers pile up one on top of another. The bottom one was laid down first, so its fossil is older.

opts: Every last one of that kind has died
quiz.why: Extinct means that kind of being is gone for ever.

quiz.p: How do scientists know when the big dinosaurs died out?
opts: Their fossils stop appearing in rocks younger than a certain age
quiz.why: Rocks form in layers, and scientists can tell how old each layer is. Big dinosaur fossils are found in older layers, and not in any layer younger than about 66 million years.

quiz.p: Which group spread into many new kinds after the big dinosaurs died out?
quiz.why: Mammals had been small. After the big dinosaurs were gone, they spread into many new kinds, including humans much later. Ammonites and pterosaurs died out.

quiz.p: Farida, a girl in Class 2, says humans are mammals. Is she right?
opts: Yes. Humans have hair and feed babies on milk
No. Mammals are only animals with four legs
quiz.why: Humans are animals, and mammals like cows, cats and elephants. We have hair and feed our babies on milk.

quiz.p: What do scientists still argue about?
opts: What made the big dinosaurs die out
Whether fossils are found in rock
quiz.why: Scientists agree dinosaurs were real and fossils are in rock. They still argue whether an asteroid, the Deccan volcanoes, or both ended the big dinosaurs.

applications: Geologists use fossils to tell the age of rock layers. Rock with the same fossils in two places was laid down at about the same time.
Coal is made from plants that lived long ago and were buried. Petrol and gas come from tiny sea beings buried long ago. This is why they are called fossil fuels.
Museums use fossils to show people what life was like long ago, like the dinosaur eggs at the Raiyoli fossil park in Gujarat.

Scientists study past extinctions to help protect animals in danger today. Cheetahs died out in India in the last century, and in 2022 cheetahs from Namibia were brought to Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh.

spotted.text: A crow or a pigeon at the window. Birds are the only dinosaurs alive today.
spotted.art: A crow sitting on a window ledge of a flat, with a faint drawing of a small feathered dinosaur behind her.

spotted.text: Some limestone steps and floors in old buildings and temples have tiny fossil shells in them. Look closely at the stone.
spotted.art: A close view of a pale stone step with tiny curled shells showing in the stone, and a child's finger pointing.

spotted.text: A conch shell or cowrie shells at home. A shell like this is the hard part that can become a fossil.
spotted.art: A white conch shell and a few cowrie shells on a wooden shelf.

spotted.text: Dinosaur models and real fossils at a science museum, like the Government Museum in Chennai or the Indroda park in Gandhinagar.

open_questions.why_open: Colour is almost never kept in fossils. For a few small feathered dinosaurs, scientists have found tiny traces in the feathers that show some colours. For most dinosaurs, nobody knows.

open_questions.q: Was it the asteroid, the Deccan volcanoes, or both, that ended the big dinosaurs?
open_questions.why_open: Both happened at about the same time. Scientists are still measuring the dates more exactly and arguing about which mattered more.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of animals lived long ago that left no fossil at all?
open_questions.why_open: Soft-bodied animals rarely leave fossils, so many kinds may have lived and vanished without a trace. Nobody can count what left nothing behind.

ask_kids: Which of the things in this room would still be here in a million years?
Look at the crow at the window. What does she have in common with a dinosaur?
If you found a bone in the ground, how would you find out who it belonged to?
Which animals alive today do you think are most like the ones who lived through the big change?
What is the oldest thing in our home? How do you know?

jokes.j: What do you call a dinosaur who is fast asleep?
What do you call a dinosaur who knows lots of words?
Why did the dinosaur cross the road?
jokes.a: Because there were no chickens yet.

jokes.j: What does a triceratops sit on?
What do dinosaurs put on their floors?
Why was the shell fossil so sure of herself?
jokes.a: Everything she said was set in stone.

jokes.j: What kind of dinosaur rides an auto in Chennai?
Why do palaeontologists never get bored?
jokes.a: There is always a bone to pick.

maths.problem: Asha did the Print Test with 8 things. 5 left clear prints, 2 left blurry prints and 1 left almost nothing. How many more clear prints than blurry prints were there? What does this tell you?
maths.answer: 3 more clear prints than blurry prints.
maths.explain: 5 take away 2 is 3. So there were 3 more clear prints. Most of the clear prints came from hard things, which tells us hard things leave better prints.
maths.context: This is about the Print Test, where you pressed hard and soft things into dough.
maths.why_maths: Counting the prints in each group shows the pattern clearly: hard things leave more clear prints.

maths.problem: A Tyrannosaurus rex was about 12 metres long. A car is about 4 metres long. How many cars, parked nose to tail, would be as long as one Tyrannosaurus rex?
maths.explain: 4 metres and 4 metres and 4 metres make 12 metres. That is 3 groups of 4. So 3 cars in a row are about as long as one Tyrannosaurus rex.
maths.context: This is about how big some dinosaurs were, compared with things we see every day.
maths.why_maths: Measuring with something we know, like a car, helps us picture how big an animal was.

maths.problem: In Footprint Detective, a girl called Revathi took slow steps 2 hand spans apart. Her quick steps were 4 hand spans apart. A scientist finds two lines of prints from the same kind of dinosaur. In one line the gaps are 2 metres, and in the other the gaps are 4 metres. Which dinosaur was moving faster?
maths.answer: The one whose prints were 4 metres apart.
maths.explain: Revathi's quick steps had the bigger gaps, 4 spans instead of 2. So bigger gaps mean faster. 4 metres is more than 2 metres, so that dinosaur was moving faster.
maths.context: This is about Footprint Detective, where you made wet footprints walking slowly and quickly.
maths.why_maths: Comparing gaps between prints lets us work out how fast an animal moved, even one who lived long ago.

founder: ideas/by_topic/evolution-the-tree-of-life.md: the timeline of life (dinosaurs about 230 million years ago, birds from dinosaurs, the dinosaur extinction 66 million years ago, mammals spreading after) shaped the explanation cards and the Who Lived Through the Big Change game. The SCI card on Mary Anning is kept for the level 4 unit, and named here in the how-we-found-out card.
No board chapters are listed for this subtopic. The unit follows the covers line: fossils as traces of old life, dinosaurs, and the animals that came after.
science: Cuvier, G. (1796). Mémoire sur les espèces d'éléphans vivantes et fossiles, read at the Institut National, Paris. Showed Indian and African elephants are different species and that the mammoth differs from both.
Alvarez, L. W., Alvarez, W., Asaro, F. and Michel, H. V. (1980). Extraterrestrial cause for the Cretaceous-Tertiary extinction. Science 208: 1095 to 1108.

Keller, G. and others: work arguing that Deccan Traps volcanism was a main cause of the end-Cretaceous extinction. Schoene, B. and others (2019), Science 363: 862 to 866, dated Deccan eruptions around the boundary.
Wilson, J. A., Sereno, P. C., Srivastava, S., Bhatt, D. K., Khosla, A. and Sahni, A. (2003). A new abelisaurid (Dinosauria, Theropoda) from the Lameta Formation of India. Rajasaurus narmadensis.

Wilson, J. A., Mohabey, D. M., Peters, S. E. and Head, J. J. (2010). Predation upon hatchling dinosaurs by a new snake from the Late Cretaceous of India. PLoS Biology 8: e1000322. Sanajeh indicus, found at Dholi Dungri, Gujarat.

Rust, J. and others (2010). Biogeographic and evolutionary implications of a diverse paleobiota in amber from the early Eocene of India. PNAS 107: 18360 to 18365. Cambay amber, about 50 to 52 million years old.
Thewissen, J. G. M. and others (2007). Whales originated from aquatic artiodactyls in the Eocene epoch of India. Nature 450: 1190 to 1194. Indohyus, from rocks collected in Kashmir by A. Ranga Rao.
Vartanyan, S. L. and others (1993). Holocene dwarf mammoths from Wrangel Island in the Siberian Arctic. Nature 362: 337 to 340. Mammoths survived there until about 4,000 years ago.

roots.context: We have pressed hard and soft things into dough, and dug down through layers. Now we ask what the rocks tell us about life, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In your dough, the key and the spoon left sharp prints, but the banana left a blurry dent. Rocks keep hard parts much better than soft bodies. Most fossils are bones, teeth, shells and wood. So the story in the rocks leaves out most soft animals, like worms and jellyfish.
deep_truth.habit: We think the fossils show us everything that lived long ago, and that no fossil means no animal. The Print Test shows that rocks keep mostly hard parts, so many soft beings lived and left no trace at all.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Print Test, every hard thing left a clear print, and every soft thing squashed into a blurry mark. Worms and jellyfish have lived for hundreds of millions of years, yet their fossils are very rare.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal and a mammal, in a family of life far older than the dinosaurs. Your thumb print in the dough is a trace of you.
three.what_is_life: Life keeps changing shape. Kinds of beings appear, live for a long time, and some die out, while others carry on as new kinds.
three.what_is_this_world: The ground under your feet was once sea floor and forest. The rocks hold traces of beings who lived there long before us.

roots.thread: Every being in the rocks once lived, sensed the world and made choices, just as the crow at the window does today. When the big dinosaurs died out, small mammals and birds spread into the empty places. Over millions of years, they became many new kinds: elephants, whales, bats and, much later, us. One family of life keeps carrying on in new shapes, even when some of its kinds are lost.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught that everything that is made will change and pass away. Seeing this clearly helps us suffer less.
teachings.link: Kinds of animals pass too. Ammonites and the big dinosaurs lived for millions of years, and then they were gone.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: Some men who cannot see each touch one part of an elephant. One feels the leg and says an elephant is like a pillar. One feels the ear and says it is like a winnowing basket. Each is sure he is right.
teachings.link: Scientists often find only a few bones of an animal. When Gideon Mantell first drew Iguanodon in the 1800s, he put a spike on the animal's nose. Whole skeletons found later showed it was a thumb spike.

teachings.teaching: The hymn asks where all of creation came from, and ends: perhaps the one who watches from the highest heaven knows, or perhaps even that one does not know.
teachings.link: Honest not-knowing is part of science too. Nobody knows for sure yet what ended the big dinosaurs.

science.text: All living beings today, and those we find as fossils, belong to one family of life with shared ancestors.
What ended the big dinosaurs: a giant asteroid, the Deccan volcanoes of India, or both together.

other_view.view: Some people believe the Earth is only a few thousand years old, so fossils cannot be millions of years old. Most scientists disagree, because many kinds of evidence agree that the Earth is very old. It is good to know that people see this differently, and to look at the evidence together.

practice.title: Thumb Print, Slow Breath
practice.say: Take a small piece of dough. Press your thumb into it, and lift it away. Look at the print your thumb left. Now sit still and breathe in slowly while I count to four. Breathe out slowly while I count to four. Do it three times, looking at the print. Your thumb has moved away, but its print is still there. Long ago, a dinosaur's foot pressed into mud just like that.
practice.kid: Press your thumb into some dough. Lift it away. Look at the print. Breathe in slowly to four. Breathe out slowly to four. Do it three times. Your thumb moved, but the print stayed.

ask: If a kind of animal died out long ago, but we can hold their bone, are they still part of our world?
Which part of you would you like the rocks to keep? Why?
The ammonites are gone, but the crow is here. What decides who carries on?
roots.art: A girl sitting cross-legged on a balcony, looking at her thumb print in a small round of dough, with a crow on the railing and a fossil ammonite on the floor beside her.

how_we_found_out.context: People once thought no kind of animal could ever die out completely. This card tells the true story of how that idea was shown wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: Before about 1800, many people in Europe thought no kind of animal could ever die out. When huge bones were dug up, they said the animals must still be alive somewhere far away. Georges Cuvier was a young scientist at the natural history museum in Paris. In 1796, he compared the teeth and jaws of elephants from India and from Africa. He showed that they were two different kinds of elephant. Then he looked at mammoth bones dug up in Siberia, in the far north of Russia. Their teeth were different from both kinds of living elephant. A mammoth was a huge animal. Travellers could not have missed herds of them. So Cuvier said that the mammoth was a kind that had died out for ever. Later, fossil hunters like Mary Anning, a young woman from a poor family in England, found many more animals that no longer lived anywhere. Today we know the last mammoths lived on Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean, until about 4,000 years ago.
how_we_found_out.who: Georges Cuvier, a French scientist in Paris (1796); later Mary Anning, a fossil hunter in Lyme Regis, England (early 1800s)
how_we_found_out.when: Cuvier read his paper on living and fossil elephants in Paris in 1796. Mary Anning made her finds from about 1811 onwards.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That no kind of animal could ever die out, so huge fossil bones must belong to animals still living somewhere unexplored. Cuvier showed the mammoth was a different kind from any living elephant, and far too big to stay hidden.

Followed the Print Test, Newspaper Pile, Footprint Detective, salt dough project and the Footprint challenge step by step in a flat: fixed the footprint paper (two lines, not one reused), the plaster of Paris idea, the drying time for the dough prints, and a food-safety note about reusing dough. Fixed the story ending that put off what the unit teaches, made-up people (Arjun was a baby brother in the story and a classmate on a worksheet), repeated questions about footprints, and cut one weak joke.
